00.01.title: Your engineering notebook
00.01.html:
This course asks you to build every tool yourself, so the first thing you build is the bench you’ll work at: a Python environment, a folder for lessons, and a test that tells you when something works. By the end of this lesson you have a repository that runs pytest and prints a green line.

The loop every lesson follows

Each lesson runs the same four steps. You derive the model by hand, write the code from nothing, prove it with a test, and keep the result in your repository. The test is the part that turns a script into engineering: it states what “correct” means before you look at the output.

What a passing artifact looks like

An artifact passes when three things hold:

  • It runs from a fresh clone with one command
  • Its test compares the result against something you trust independently: a hand calculation, an analytic limit, or a conservation law
  • The tolerance in the test is justified, not tuned until it passes

The third point is the one people skip. If your test says abs(x - 3.0) < 0.5 because 0.5 made it pass, the test proves nothing. Later lessons show you how to pick tolerances from the size of truncation and round-off error.

Setting up the environment

You need Python 3.10 or newer. A virtual environment keeps this course’s packages separate from everything else on your machine, so an upgrade elsewhere can’t break a lesson you finished months ago.

The repository layout stays the same for the whole course: lesson code in lessons/, tests in tests/, one file per lesson.

Worked exampleChecking your toolchain with a real test

The smoke test below checks two things you’ll rely on constantly: that NumPy is installed, and that floating-point arithmetic behaves the way IEEE 754 says it should. The sum 0.1+0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in binary floating point; the difference is 5.55×10−17, one unit in the last place of a number near 0.3. A test that compares with == would fail here, which is why every numeric test in this course uses a tolerance.

With ε=2−52≈2.22×10−16 (machine epsilon for doubles), the error is ε/4, so a tolerance of 10−12 is safe by four orders of magnitude.

Run it with python smoke_test.py, then with pytest -q. Both should pass. Commit the file: it’s your first artifact.

Exercise 1Write a test that fails for the right reason

Write a function mean(xs) and a test for it. Then deliberately break the function (for example, divide by len(xs) + 1) and confirm the test fails. What tolerance did you use for the comparison, and why?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A correct implementation is def mean(xs): return sum(xs) / len(xs).
  2. Test it against a case you can compute by hand: mean([1, 2, 3, 4]) is exactly 2.5. The inputs are small integers, so the sum is exact in floating point and you can use a tight tolerance such as 1e-12.
  3. The broken version returns 10/5=2.0, an error of 0.5, far outside 10−12, so the test fails.
  4. The tolerance is justified because the only error source is the final division, which is accurate to within half a unit in the last place (about 2.8×10−16 for 2.5).

Exercise 2Make the repository reproducible

Add a requirements.txt that pins the package versions you installed, then recreate the environment in a new folder and run the smoke test there.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Run pip freeze > requirements.txt inside the activated environment.
  2. In a new folder: python3 -m venv .venv, activate it, then pip install -r requirements.txt.
  3. Copy smoke_test.py across and run pytest -q. A pass shows the environment is reproducible from the file alone.

00.02.title: SI units and why rockets crash
00.02.html:
Most wrong answers in engineering are not bad math; they are numbers in the wrong unit. In this lesson you treat a unit as part of the number, write a Quantity class that refuses to add metres to seconds, and see how one missing conversion destroyed a spacecraft.

A unit is a vector of exponents

Every SI quantity can be written as a number times a product of the seven base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. A newton is kgms−2; a pascal is kgm−1s−2. If you store only the exponents, a unit becomes a vector of seven integers:

[N]=(1,1,−2,0,0,0,0)over (m,kg,s,A,K,mol,cd)

Unit algebra then reduces to vector algebra:

  • Multiplying quantities adds their exponent vectors
  • Dividing subtracts them
  • Raising to a power p multiplies the vector by p
  • Adding or subtracting is allowed only when the vectors are equal

That last rule is the whole point. A sum of a length and a time is not small or large; it is meaningless, and your code should say so.

The Mars Climate Orbiter

In September 1999 NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter. The mishap investigation board found that ground software produced thruster impulse data in pound-force seconds, while the navigation software expected newton seconds. One pound-force second is 4.448 newton seconds, so every small trajectory correction was under-counted by that factor. The accumulated error put the spacecraft far lower at Mars than planned, and it was lost on arrival.

No equation was wrong. The bug was a number travelling between two programs without its unit.

Worked exampleConverting impulse correctly

A thruster burn delivers an impulse of J=12.0 lbfs. With 1 lbf=4.448222 N:

J=12.0×4.448222 Ns=53.38 Ns

If software reads the raw number 12.0 as newton seconds, the recorded impulse is 12.0 N s, low by a factor of 4.448. For a 338 kg spacecraft the velocity change Δv=J/m is 53.38/338=0.158 m/s, but the software books 12.0/338=0.0355 m/s.

Writing the Quantity class

The class stores a float and an exponent tuple. Arithmetic operators combine exponents; addition checks them first. Keeping the exponents as a tuple of integers (or fractions, for square roots) makes equality checks exact.

Torque versus energy

A newton-metre of torque and a joule of energy have identical exponent vectors. Dimensional checks catch “metres plus seconds” but cannot catch “torque plus energy”. Engineers keep the unit names different (N m versus J) as a reminder; your code can add a tag if you need that distinction.

Exercise 1Pressure in a Swiss dam

Water at the base of a 250 m deep reservoir is under hydrostatic pressure p=ρgh. Using your Quantity class with ρ=1000 kg/m3 and g=9.81 m/s2, compute p and confirm the result has the exponents of a pascal. Express it in bar (1 bar=105 Pa).

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Build the inputs: rho = q(1000, kg=1, m=-3), g = q(9.81, m=1, s=-2), h = q(250, m=1).
  2. Multiply: exponents add to (−3+1+1, 1, −2)=(−1,1,−2) over (m, kg, s), which is kgm−1s−2, a pascal.
  3. Value: 1000×9.81×250=2.4525×106 Pa.
  4. In bar: 2.4525×106/105=24.5 bar, about 24 times atmospheric pressure.

sections.title: A unit is a vector of exponents

quiz.q: In exponent-vector form, what happens to units when you divide two quantities?
quiz.explain: Division subtracts exponents: m/s is (1,0,−1).

quiz.q: Convert an impulse of 12.0 lbfs to newton seconds (1 lbf=4.448222 N).
quiz.explain: 12.0×4.448222=53.38 Ns.

quiz.explain: p=ρgh=2.4525×106 Pa=24.5 bar.

quiz.explain: Both are kgm2s−2; dimensional analysis alone can’t separate them.

quiz.explain: Ground software output lbf·s while navigation expected N·s, under-counting impulse by a factor of 4.45.

Impulse data in pound-force seconds read as newton seconds

00.03.title: Dimensional analysis and Buckingham Pi
00.03.html:
Before you solve anything, you can often predict the shape of the answer from units alone. Dimensional analysis tells you which combinations of variables can appear in a physical law, how many independent ones there are, and how to scale a model test up to the real machine.

The dimension matrix

Write each variable as a column of exponents over the base dimensions mass M, length L and time T. For a pendulum with period Tp​, length ℓ, gravity g, bob mass m and release angle θ0​:

A=MLT​Tp​001​ℓ010​g01−2​m100​θ0​000​​

A product Tpa​ℓbgcmdθ0e​ is dimensionless exactly when its exponent vector x=(a,b,c,d,e) satisfies

Ax=0.

So the dimensionless groups are the null space of A. That’s the whole theorem in one line.

The Buckingham Pi theorem

If a physical law involves n variables and the dimension matrix has rank r, the law can be rewritten as a relation between n−r independent dimensionless groups Π1​,…,Πn−r​:

f(Π1​,Π2​,…,Πn−r​)=0.

For the pendulum, n=5 and r=3, so there are two groups. Solving Ax=0 gives Π1​=Tp​g/ℓ​ and Π2​=θ0​. Mass appears in no group, so the period can’t depend on it. Therefore

Tp​=gℓ​​ϕ(θ0​).

Units alone told you the ℓ/g​ scaling. They can’t tell you that ϕ(0)=2π; for that you need the differential equation, which you’ll solve in lesson 01.08.

Drag and the Reynolds number

Drag force F on a body of size D moving at speed v through a fluid of density ρ and viscosity μ gives n=5, r=3, so again two groups:

C=ρv2D2F​,Re=μρvD​=νvD​,

and the law must have the form C=ϕ(Re). Two geometrically similar bodies at the same Reynolds number have the same force coefficient. That is the basis of every wind tunnel and towing tank.

Worked exampleTesting a car in a water tunnel

A 1:10 scale model of a car that drives at 100 km/h in air (νa​=1.5×10−5 m2/s, ρa​=1.2 kg/m3) is tested in water (νw​=1.0×10−6 m2/s, ρw​=1000 kg/m3). What speed matches the Reynolds number, and how does the measured force scale?

  1. Match Re: vm​Dm​/νw​=vp​Dp​/νa​, so vm​=vp​Dm​Dp​​νa​νw​​=100×10×151​=66.7 km/h.
  2. In air the model would need 1000 km/h, close to the speed of sound, where compressibility adds a new group (the Mach number). Water avoids that.
  3. Equal Re means equal C, so Fm​/Fp​=ρa​vp2​Dp2​ρw​vm2​Dm2​​=1.21000​×(1.51​)2×1001​=3.70.

The small model in water feels 3.7 times the drag of the full car in air. Divide the measured force by 3.70 to predict the real one.

Computing Pi groups in code

The null space can be computed numerically with the singular value decomposition: the right singular vectors whose singular values are zero span it. The code below does that, then also computes an exact rational basis by Gaussian elimination so you get clean exponents like 1/2 instead of 0.7071.

For drag, the exact routine returns F/(ρv2D2) and Fρ/μ2. The second one is CRe2. Any product or power of Pi groups is also a valid group, so you are free to swap it for Re; the theorem fixes how many groups there are, not which ones you pick.

Exercise 1Pressure drop in a pipe

The pressure drop Δp along a pipe depends on density ρ, viscosity μ, mean velocity v, diameter D, length L and wall roughness ε. How many dimensionless groups govern the problem? Propose a set.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Count variables: Δp,ρ,μ,v,D,L,ε, so n=7.
  2. The dimensions involved are M, L, T and ρ,v,D alone already have rank 3, so r=3.
  3. Number of groups: n−r=4.
  4. A natural set uses ρ,v,D as repeating variables: ρv2Δp​, Re=μρvD​, DL​ and Dε​.
  5. Since Δp grows linearly with length in a long pipe, this becomes the Darcy form ρv2/2Δp​=f(Re,Dε​)DL​, which you’ll meet again in Phase 11.

Exercise 2A taller pendulum

A pendulum clock beats with period 2.0 s. Using only the scaling Tp​∝ℓ​, by what factor must its length change to give a period of 3.0 s?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At fixed θ0​ and g, Tp​=ℓ/g​ϕ(θ0​), so Tp​∝ℓ​.
  2. ℓ2​/ℓ1​=(T2​/T1​)2=(3.0/2.0)2=2.25.
  3. The pendulum must be 2.25 times longer. No value of ϕ was needed.

quiz.q: A law involves 7 variables and the dimension matrix has rank 3. How many independent dimensionless groups are there?
quiz.explain: Buckingham Pi: n−r=7−3=4.

quiz.q: In matrix terms, the exponent vectors of dimensionless groups are…
quiz.explain: A product is dimensionless when Ax=0, which is the definition of the null space.
options: The null space of the dimension matrix
The eigenvectors of the dimension matrix
The column space of the dimension matrix
The rows of the dimension matrix

quiz.q: Using Tp​=2πℓ/g​ with g=9.81 m/s2, what is the small-swing period of a 2.5 m pendulum?
quiz.explain: 2π2.5/9.81​=3.17 s.

quiz.q: A 1:20 ship model is tested in the same water as the ship, matching Froude number v/gL​. If the ship sails at 10 m/s, what is the model speed?
quiz.explain: Equal v/gL​ means vm​=vp​Lm​/Lp​​=10/20​=2.24 m/s.

quiz.q: Why can’t a pendulum’s period depend on the bob mass?
quiz.explain: No other variable carries M, so no dimensionless combination can include m.
options: Mass is the only variable with dimension M, so it can’t appear in any dimensionless group
Heavier bobs fall faster and lighter ones slower, which averages out
It does depend on mass, weakly

00.04.title: Estimation and Fermi problems
00.04.html:
A good engineer can say “about ten thousand cubic metres a day” before opening a spreadsheet, and know how wrong that might be. In this lesson you estimate a quantity as a product of rough factors, put honest error bars on it, and check the error bars with a Monte Carlo simulation.

Break the unknown into factors you can bound

Take a Subak irrigation canal in Bali, the kind that feeds terraced rice fields. How much water passes a point in one day? You don’t know, but you can bound the pieces:

  • Width w: somewhere between 0.4 and 1.6 m, best guess 0.8 m
  • Depth d: between 0.15 and 0.6 m, best guess 0.3 m
  • Mean flow speed v: between 0.25 and 1 m/s, best guess 0.5 m/s

Volume per day is

V=wdvt=0.8×0.3×0.5×86400≈1.04×104 m3.

When a guess is “within a factor of 2”, use logs

Each bound above is “best guess, times or divided by 2”. Errors like that are multiplicative, so they live naturally on a log scale. If each factor is xi​=x^i​kui​ with ui​ uniform on [−1,1], then

lnV=i∑​lnx^i​+lnki∑​ui​.

A uniform variable on [−1,1] has standard deviation 1/3​. Independent errors add in quadrature, so with m uncertain factors

σlnV​=lnk3m​​.

With m=3 uncertain factors and k=2: σlnV​=ln2=0.693. A central 90% interval spans about ±1.645σ in log space, a factor of e1.645×0.693=3.1 either side. Two lessons follow:

  1. The uncertainty of a product grows like m​, not m. Errors partly cancel.
  2. When the low and high guesses differ by a lot, the best single number is their geometric mean xlow​xhigh​​, not the arithmetic mean.

Worked exampleDaily flow, with error bars

Estimate the daily volume and a 90% interval, treating width, depth and speed as uncertain by a factor of 2 each.

  1. Point estimate: 0.8×0.3×0.5×86400=10368 m3.
  2. Log spread: σ=ln23/3​=0.693.
  3. 90% factor: e1.645×0.693=3.13.
  4. Interval: 10368/3.13≈3300 to 10368×3.13≈32000 m3 per day.

Report it as “about 104 m3 per day, likely between 3 000 and 30 000”. That’s a sentence someone can design a weir with.

Monte Carlo as a check on the algebra

The quadrature formula assumes independent errors and leans on the central limit theorem with only three terms. Sampling is the honest check: draw thousands of random input sets, compute V for each and read off the percentiles.

The simulated 90% factor comes out within a few percent of the hand value of 3.1, even with only three factors. The algebra was good enough.

Exercise 1Hot water for a Zurich flat

Estimate the energy a household of 4 uses per year to heat shower and tap water. Assume 40 litres of hot water per person per day, heated by 40 K, with c=4186 J/(kgK). Give the answer in kWh.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Mass per day: 4×40 L=160 kg.
  2. Energy per day: Q=mcΔT=160×4186×40=2.68×107 J.
  3. In kWh: 2.68×107/3.6×106=7.44 kWh per day.
  4. Per year: 7.44×365≈2720 kWh, roughly 3000 kWh.
  5. Sanity check: Swiss statistics put hot water at a few thousand kWh per household per year, so the estimate is the right order of magnitude.

When a guess is “within a factor of 2”, use logs
Monte Carlo as a check on the algebra

quiz.explain: The geometric mean 10×1000​=100 sits in the middle on a log axis.

quiz.q: A canal is 0.8 m wide and 0.3 m deep with a mean speed of 0.5 m/s. What volume flows past in one day?
quiz.explain: 0.8×0.3×0.5×86400=10368 m3.

quiz.q: You multiply 9 independent factors, each uncertain by the same factor. Compared with a single factor, the log-spread of the product is roughly…
quiz.explain: Independent log errors add in quadrature: 9​=3.

00.05.title: Vectors, arrays and broadcasting
00.05.html:
Forces, velocities and displacements are vectors, and an engineering model is usually thousands of them at once. In this lesson you treat a vector as a list of numbers in Rn, learn which operations are element-wise and which aren’t, and replace slow Python loops with NumPy array operations that give the same answer much faster.

Vectors as arrays

A force in the plane is a pair F=(Fx​,Fy​). Adding forces adds components; scaling a force scales each component:

F1​+F2​=(F1x​+F2x​, F1y​+F2y​),cF=(cFx​, cFy​).

Those two operations, with the usual rules, are what make Rn a vector space. Two more operations matter constantly:

a⋅b=i∑​ai​bi​,∥a∥=a⋅a​.

The dot product of force and displacement is work. The norm is a magnitude.

Element-wise is not matrix multiplication

In NumPy, a * b multiplies element by element. Matrix multiplication is a @ b. For two vectors, (a * b).sum() equals a @ b, but for matrices the two differ completely. Mixing them up is the most common array bug in engineering code, and it’s silent: both run, one is wrong.

Broadcasting

When two arrays have different shapes, NumPy stretches dimensions of length 1 to match. Shapes are compared from the right; each pair must be equal or contain a 1.

(3,1) with (1,4)⟶(3,4)

Broadcasting is how you compute all pairwise differences between N points without a loop: d = p[:, None, :] - p[None, :, :] has shape (N,N,2).

Worked exampleResultant of three forces on a bracket

A bracket carries F1​=400 N at 30∘, F2​=250 N at 120∘ and F3​=300 N at 250∘, angles measured from the x axis. Find the resultant.

  1. Components, F(cosθ,sinθ): F1​=(346.4, 200.0), F2​=(−125.0, 216.5), F3​=(−102.6, −281.9) newtons.
  2. Sum: R=(118.8, 134.6) N.
  3. Magnitude: ∥R∥=118.82+134.62​=179.5 N.
  4. Direction: atan2(134.6,118.8)=48.6∘.

In NumPy that’s three lines: build an array of shape (3,2), sum along axis 0, take the norm.

Loops versus arrays

The code computes a spring force pulling each of 105 particles toward the origin, plus gravity, once with a Python loop and once with arrays. It asserts that both agree to 10−12 and measures the speed-up.

On a laptop the vectorised version is typically 20 to 100 times faster (26 times on the machine that built this page). The physics didn’t change; the work just moved from the Python interpreter into compiled loops over contiguous memory.

Exercise 1Work done by a cable

A cable pulls a cart with force F=(120, 50, 0) N while it moves by d=(3, −2, 0.5) m. How much work does the cable do? Write it as a single NumPy expression.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Work is the dot product: W=F⋅d=120×3+50×(−2)+0×0.5.
  2. W=360−100+0=260 J.
  3. In NumPy: np.array([120, 50, 0]) @ np.array([3, -2, 0.5]) returns 260.0.
  4. Note F * d would return the array [360, -100, 0], which is not work until you sum it.

quiz.q: What shape results from broadcasting arrays of shape (5, 1) and (3,)?
quiz.explain: Align from the right: (5,1) and (1,3) stretch to (5,3).

quiz.q: Two forces act on a pin: (300,0) N and (0,400) N. What is the magnitude of the resultant?
quiz.explain: 3002+4002​=500 N.

quiz.q: Work done by F=(120,50,0) N over a displacement d=(3,−2,0.5) m.
quiz.explain: F⋅d=360−100+0=260 J.

quiz.q: For two 3×3 NumPy arrays A and B, what does A * B compute?
quiz.explain: * is element-wise. Use A @ B for the matrix product.
options: The dot product of their first rows

00.06.title: Plotting like an engineer
00.06.html:
A plot is an argument. An engineering plot has units on both axes, a scale chosen so the physics is visible, and a fit you can read off by eye. This lesson is about one trick that pays off for the rest of the course: log-log axes turn power laws into straight lines.

Power laws become lines

Many engineering relations are power laws, y=axb: drag grows with v2, fan power with speed cubed, beam deflection with length cubed, numerical error with step size to some order. Take logs of both sides:

logy=loga+blogx.

On log-log axes this is a straight line with slope b and intercept loga. The exponent, which is usually the physics you care about, becomes a slope you can measure with a ruler. From any two points,

b=logx2​−logx1​logy2​−logy1​​.

Rules for a plot someone else can use

  1. Label every axis with quantity and unit: “pressure drop, kPa”, never just “dp”.
  2. Use log axes when the data spans more than about one decade, or when you expect a power law.
  3. Show measured data as markers and models as lines, so the reader can tell what’s real.
  4. Start a linear axis at zero only when zero means something for the comparison.
  5. Put the plot’s conclusion in the caption: “error falls with h2”, not “error vs h”.

Worked exampleThe fan laws from two measurements

A cooling fan draws 12 W at 1000 rpm and 96 W at 2000 rpm. Find the exponent and predict the power at 1500 rpm.

  1. Slope on log-log axes: b=ln2000−ln1000ln96−ln12​=ln2ln8​=3.0.
  2. That’s the fan affinity law P∝n3: flow scales with speed, pressure with speed squared, and power is their product.
  3. Prediction: P=12×(1500/1000)3=12×3.375=40.5 W.

Halving the speed of a fan cuts its power by a factor of 8. That’s why variable-speed drives save so much energy.

Fitting a power law in code

With many noisy points, fit the line by least squares in log space. For points (Xi​,Yi​)=(lnxi​,lnyi​) the slope is

b=∑(Xi​−Xˉ)2∑(Xi​−Xˉ)(Yi​−Yˉ)​,lna=Yˉ−bXˉ.

Fitting the line in log space treats the scatter as a percentage, which matches how most measurement errors behave. A straight fit on linear axes would let the largest values dominate.

Exercise 1Read the order of a method

A numerical method has error 2.0×10−3 with step h=0.1 and 2.0×10−7 with h=0.001. What is its order, the exponent p in error ∝hp? What error do you expect at h=0.01?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Slope on log-log axes: p=log10​0.1−log10​0.001log10​(2×10−3)−log10​(2×10−7)​=24​=2.
  2. Second order: dividing h by 10 divides the error by 100.
  3. At h=0.01: 2.0×10−3/100=2.0×10−5.

Fitting a power law in code

quiz.explain: 12×1.53=40.5 W.

00.07.title: Error, precision and floating point
00.07.html:
Your computer doesn’t store real numbers. It stores a finite set of binary fractions, and every operation rounds to the nearest one. Most of the time that’s invisible. Sometimes it wipes out every correct digit of an answer. This lesson shows when, why, and how to rewrite a formula so it doesn’t happen.

How a double is stored

An IEEE 754 double has a sign bit, an 11-bit exponent and a 52-bit fraction:

x=(−1)s×1.f1​f2​…f52​×2e−1023.

The gap between 1 and the next representable number is machine epsilon,

ε=2−52≈2.22×10−16.

Every basic operation is exact, then rounded: fl(a∘b)=(a∘b)(1+δ) with ∣δ∣≤ε/2. So each operation costs at most about 16 significant decimal digits of relative accuracy, which sounds like plenty.

Absolute and relative error

If x^ approximates x, the absolute error is ∣x^−x∣ and the relative error is ∣x^−x∣/∣x∣. Relative error is the one that counts significant digits: 3.14 for π has relative error 5.1×10−4, about three and a half correct digits.

Catastrophic cancellation

Subtracting two nearly equal numbers is exact, but it exposes the rounding errors they already carried. If a and b each have relative error ε and agree in their first k digits, then a−b has only about 16−k correct digits left.

Take f(x)=(1−cosx)/x2, which tends to 1/2 as x→0. For x=10−8, cosx=1−5×10−17, which rounds to exactly 1. The numerator becomes 0 and the result is 0 instead of 0.5: a 100% error from a formula that is algebraically perfect.

The fix is to remove the subtraction with an identity before computing:

1−cosx=2sin22x​⟹f(x)=x22sin2(x/2)​.

No nearly equal numbers are subtracted, so the result is accurate to machine precision for every x.

Worked exampleThe quadratic formula that loses a root

Solve x2−108x+1=0. The roots are close to 108 and 10−8.

  1. Textbook formula for the small root: x2​=2b−b2−4​​ with b=108. Here b2−4​ agrees with b to 16 digits, so the subtraction cancels them all. In double precision it returns 7.45×10−9, a 25% error.
  2. Better: compute the large root without cancellation, x1​=2b+b2−4​​, then use x1​x2​=c/a=1 (Vieta).
  3. x2​=1/x1​=b+b2−4​2​=1.000×10−8, correct to every digit.

The physics behind numbers like these is real: a stiff spring next to a soft one, or a tiny damping term next to a large stiffness, produces exactly this kind of quadratic.

Rules of thumb

  1. Look for subtractions of nearly equal quantities and rewrite them with identities, conjugates or series.
  2. Never test floats with ==; compare with a tolerance like abs(a - b) <= rtol * abs(b).
  3. Sum many small numbers with care (lesson 01.14 builds compensated summation).
  4. Expect about 15 to 16 significant digits at best, and fewer after every cancellation.

Exercise 1A stable square-root difference

For large x, g(x)=x+1​−x​ suffers cancellation. Rewrite it so it’s accurate, and evaluate it at x=1012.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Multiply and divide by the conjugate: x+1​−x​=x+1​+x​(x+1)−x​=x+1​+x​1​.
  2. The new form adds positive numbers only, so no digits cancel.
  3. At x=1012: 106+1061​=5.0×10−7 (more precisely 4.99999999999875×10−7).
  4. The naive form keeps only about 5 correct digits here (relative error 7.6×10−6), because the two square roots agree to 12 digits.

quiz.q: What is machine epsilon 2−52 for IEEE doubles?
quiz.explain: 2−52≈2.22×10−16.

quiz.q: Relative error of 3.14 as an approximation of π.
quiz.explain: ∣3.14−π∣/π=5.07×10−4.

quiz.q: In double precision, what does (1−cosx)/x2 return for x=10−8?
quiz.explain: cos(10−8) rounds to exactly 1, so the numerator is 0.

quiz.q: Using the stable form 1/(x+1​+x​), evaluate x+1​−x​ at x=1012.
quiz.explain: 1/(2×106)=5×10−7.

quiz.q: How should you check whether two computed floats are equal?
quiz.explain: Compare with a tolerance scaled to the size of the numbers.

00.08.title: Reading data from sensors
00.08.html:
Real data arrives late, irregular and noisy. A river gauge logs every ten minutes, except when the modem drops out; a thermocouple reports volts, not degrees. This lesson turns raw readings into a clean, evenly spaced series you can trust: convert units, interpolate onto a regular grid, and avoid the sampling mistake that makes fast signals look slow.

From signal to physical value

Industrial sensors usually send a 4 to 20 mA current loop. Zero current means a broken wire, which is why the scale starts at 4. A linear sensor maps current I to a quantity y with

y=ymin​+16 mAI−4 mA​(ymax​−ymin​).

Calibrating a sensor means finding that straight line from two or more known points, then checking the residuals.

Sampling and aliasing

Sampling at rate fs​ can only represent frequencies up to the Nyquist frequency fs​/2. A sinusoid at frequency f above that doesn’t disappear; it shows up at the alias

falias​=∣f−kfs​∣,k=round(f/fs​).

A 0.9 Hz vibration sampled once per second looks like a slow 0.1 Hz drift. No amount of processing afterwards can tell the two apart, which is why data loggers put an analogue low-pass filter before the converter.

Resampling with linear interpolation

To put irregular samples (ti​,yi​) onto an hourly grid, find for each grid time t the two neighbours ti​≤t≤ti+1​ and interpolate:

y(t)=yi​+ti+1​−ti​t−ti​​(yi+1​−yi​).

Linear interpolation never overshoots the data and preserves the mean of a smooth signal well. It can’t recover anything faster than the original sampling, and it quietly bridges gaps, so the code also reports the longest gap it bridged.

Worked exampleA level gauge on the Limmat

A pressure-based level sensor on the Limmat in Zurich spans 0 to 5 m over 4 to 20 mA and samples every 10 minutes.

  1. A reading of 11.2 mA means y=0+1611.2−4​×5=2.25 m.
  2. Nyquist limit: fs​=1/600 Hz, so fs​/2=1/1200 Hz: anything faster than one cycle per 20 minutes is unresolved. Surface waves are, river level changes from rain and lake regulation are not.
  3. Two neighbouring samples at 10:00 (2.20 m) and 10:10 (2.26 m) give 2.236 m at 10:06, by 2.20+0.6×0.06.

Notice that the raw mean is computed as a time-weighted average (trapezoids between samples), not a plain average of readings. With irregular sampling a plain average over-weights the periods when the logger happened to sample more often.

Exercise 1Choose a sample rate

A pump’s shaft runs at 2950 rpm and you want to see vibration up to the third harmonic of shaft speed. What is the minimum sampling rate, and what rate would you actually choose?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Shaft frequency: 2950/60=49.2 Hz.
  2. Third harmonic: 3×49.2=147.5 Hz.
  3. Nyquist requires fs​>2×147.5=295 Hz.
  4. Real anti-alias filters roll off gradually, so choose 2.5 to 4 times the highest frequency: a standard 1 kHz rate is a sensible choice.

quiz.q: A 4 to 20 mA level sensor spans 0 to 5 m. What level does a reading of 11.2 mA mean?
quiz.explain: (11.2−4)/16×5=2.25 m.

quiz.q: A 0.9 Hz vibration is sampled at 1 Hz. At what frequency does it appear?
quiz.explain: ∣0.9−1×1∣=0.1 Hz.

quiz.q: Samples read 2.20 m at 10:00 and 2.26 m at 10:10. What does linear interpolation give at 10:06?
quiz.explain: 2.20+0.6×0.06=2.236 m.

quiz.q: Why does a 4 to 20 mA loop start at 4 mA and not 0?
quiz.explain: A live zero lets the receiver detect a fault.
options: Because sensors can’t produce less than 4 mA
It’s an arbitrary historical choice with no use
So a broken wire (0 mA) is distinguishable from a zero reading

quiz.q: With irregular samples, how should you compute the mean level over a period?
quiz.explain: Weight each value by the time it represents.
options: Use only the first and last readings
Time-weighted average, for example trapezoids between samples

00.09.title: Version control for engineers
00.09.html:
Engineering work is a chain of decisions, and you need to know which version of a calculation produced which drawing. Git solves that with one idea: name every file and every snapshot by a hash of its content. In this lesson you build that idea yourself in about 30 lines, then see why it makes history tamper-evident and bugs findable in a handful of steps.

A hash is a fingerprint

A cryptographic hash function maps any sequence of bytes to a fixed-size number, 160 bits for SHA-1 as used by classic git. Two properties matter:

  1. The same content always gives the same hash.
  2. Changing a single byte changes the hash completely and unpredictably.

Git names a file’s content (“blob”) by

id=SHA1("blob "∥length∥\0∥content).

A directory (“tree”) is a list of names and the ids of what they contain, hashed in turn. A commit is a hash of a tree id, the parent commit id, the author and the message. So a commit id is a hash of hashes all the way down: change any byte of any file in history and every id after it changes.

How unlikely is a collision?

With n objects and a b-bit hash, the birthday bound gives the probability that any two collide:

p≈2b+1n2​.

For a million files and b=160, p≈1012/2161=3.4×10−37. Accidental collisions are not a practical concern. Deliberate SHA-1 collisions have been shown, which is why git is moving to SHA-256; the idea stays the same.

Finding the commit that broke something

If a test passed at commit 0 and fails at commit N, git bisect checks the middle, keeps the half that contains the change, and repeats. It’s the bisection method you’ll meet again in lesson 01.02, applied to history, and it needs only

⌈log2​N⌉

test runs. A thousand commits take ten.

Worked exampleThe id of a file containing “hello”

Compute the git blob id of a file whose content is the six bytes hello plus a newline.

  1. Header: blob 6 followed by a zero byte.
  2. Hash the header plus content with SHA-1.
  3. Result: ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a.

Run echo hello | git hash-object --stdin in any terminal and you get the same 40 hex digits. Your 30 lines and git agree because they implement the same definition.

The store writes objects in the same compressed format and folder layout git uses under .git/objects. Point it at a real repository and get can read git’s own blobs.

Exercise 1Bisect a regression

Your beam solver’s test passed in March and fails today, 600 commits later. Each test run takes 4 minutes. Roughly how long does a bisect take, compared with testing every commit?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Number of runs: ⌈log2​600⌉=10, since 29=512<600≤1024=210.
  2. Bisect time: 10×4=40 minutes.
  3. Testing every commit: up to 600×4=2400 minutes, 40 hours.
  4. Bisect is 60 times faster here, and the advantage grows with history length.

sections.title: Finding the commit that broke something

quiz.q: How many test runs does bisection need, at most, to find the bad commit among 1000?
quiz.explain: ⌈log2​1000⌉=10.

quiz.q: You change one character in a file deep in an old commit. What happens to the ids?
quiz.explain: Every object stores the hashes below it, so the change propagates upward and forward.
options: The blob, every tree above it, that commit and every later commit change
Only that file’s blob id changes

quiz.q: Birthday-bound collision probability n2/2b+1 for n=106 objects and a 160-bit hash.
quiz.explain: 1012/2161=3.4×10−37.

quiz.q: Two engineers commit files with identical content. How many blob objects does git store?
quiz.explain: Objects are named by content, so identical content is stored once.
options: It depends on the file names

00.10.title: Free-body thinking before formulas
00.10.html:
Every mechanics problem in this course starts the same way: cut the object you care about free from everything it touches, replace each contact with the force it transmits, and only then write equations. Skip the drawing and you will forget a force, double-count one, or get a sign wrong. This lesson makes that habit concrete and checkable in code.

Newton’s laws as balance statements

For a body at rest, or moving at constant velocity, Newton’s first law says the forces and moments on it balance. In the plane that’s three scalar equations:

∑Fx​=0,∑Fy​=0,∑MO​=0.

The moment about a point O of a force F applied at r (measured from O) is the 2D cross product

MO​=rx​Fy​−ry​Fx​.

Three equations means you can find at most three unknown forces on one rigid body in the plane. If a diagram has more unknowns, the body is statically indeterminate and you’ll need deformation (Phase 06) to solve it.

The four-step recipe

  1. Isolate: draw only the body, with its outline cut free.
  2. Replace: at every cut, draw the force the removed part exerted. A smooth surface pushes perpendicular to itself; a rough one adds a friction force along it; a pin can push in any direction (two unknowns); a fixed clamp adds a moment too.
  3. Load: add gravity at the centre of mass and any applied loads.
  4. Balance: write the three equations, choosing the moment point where unknowns meet so they drop out.

Worked exampleWill the ladder slip?

A uniform ladder of length L=4 m and mass 15 kg leans against a smooth wall at θ=60∘ to the floor. What wall reaction and floor friction keep it in place, and what friction coefficient is needed?

  1. Weight: W=15×9.81=147.15 N, acting at L/2.
  2. Vertical balance: Nf​=W=147.15 N.
  3. Moments about the foot, where Nf​ and F act, so they drop out: Nw​Lsinθ−W2L​cosθ=0, so Nw​=2tanθW​=2×1.732147.15​=42.5 N.
  4. Horizontal balance: F=Nw​=42.5 N.
  5. Friction needed: μ≥F/Nf​=2tanθ1​=0.289.

The ladder’s length and mass cancel out of the friction requirement. Only the angle matters, which is why ladder labels specify an angle and not a weight limit for slipping.

Checking a diagram in code

A free-body diagram is just a list of forces with application points. The code below stores it that way, solves for the unknown magnitudes with a 3×3 linear system, and then checks that every equation balances to 10−9. If you forget a force, the check fails.

Exercise 1Someone climbs the ladder

An 80 kg person stands 3 m along the same ladder (measured from the foot). What friction coefficient is now needed?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Weights: ladder Wl​=147.15 N at 2 m, person Wp​=80×9.81=784.8 N at 3 m.
  2. Moments about the foot: Nw​Lsinθ=(Wl​⋅2+Wp​⋅3)cosθ.
  3. Nw​=4×0.866(294.3+2354.4)×0.5​=382.3 N.
  4. Vertical: Nf​=147.15+784.8=931.95 N; horizontal: F=Nw​=382.3 N.
  5. μ≥382.3/931.95=0.410. The higher the climber, the more friction is needed, which is why ladders slip when someone is near the top.

quiz.q: A uniform ladder leans on a smooth wall at θ=60∘ to the floor. What minimum floor friction coefficient prevents slipping?
quiz.explain: μ=1/(2tan60∘)=0.289.

quiz.q: Same ladder: 15 kg, 4 m long, 60∘. What is the horizontal wall reaction?
quiz.explain: Nw​=W/(2tanθ)=147.15/3.464=42.5 N.

quiz.q: How many independent equilibrium equations does one rigid body in the plane give?
quiz.explain: Two force balances and one moment balance.
options: As many as there are forces

quiz.q: Which reaction can a smooth wall exert on a ladder?
quiz.explain: No friction means no tangential force.
options: A force along the wall only
A force perpendicular to the wall only

quiz.q: Moment about the origin of F=(0,−100) N applied at r=(2,1) m, using M=rx​Fy​−ry​Fx​.
quiz.explain: 2×(−100)−1×0=−200 Nm, clockwise.

00.11.title: Symbolic math as a checker
00.11.html:
Deriving by hand is how you understand a result. It’s also where sign errors and dropped factors hide. A computer algebra system such as SymPy can’t tell you what to derive, but it can tell you in a second whether your derivation is right. In this course the rule is: derive on paper first, then let the machine check you.

Equal means “the difference simplifies to zero”

Two expressions a(x) and b(x) are the same function when a−b=0 for every x. SymPy’s simplify(a - b) == 0 tries algebraic rewrites until the difference vanishes. If it returns 0, your result is proven. If it returns something else, either you made a mistake or SymPy couldn’t find the simplification, so you follow up with a numeric spot check at random points.

A derivative you can’t look up quickly

Differentiate y=xx for x>0. Neither the power rule (which needs a constant exponent) nor the exponential rule (which needs a constant base) applies. Take logs first:

lny=xlnx.

Differentiate both sides with the chain rule on the left and the product rule on the right:

yy′​=lnx+1⟹y′=xx(lnx+1).

At x=2: y′=4(ln2+1)=6.773. This technique, logarithmic differentiation, appears again whenever a variable sits in an exponent, for example in the Arrhenius law for creep.

Worked exampleA cantilever’s deflection, derived then checked

A cantilever of length L is clamped at x=0 and loaded by P at the tip. Euler–Bernoulli beam theory gives the bending moment M(x)=−P(L−x) and EIw′′(x)=M(x), with w(0)=w′(0)=0.

  1. Integrate once: EIw′=−P(Lx−2x2​)+C1​, and w′(0)=0 gives C1​=0.
  2. Integrate again: EIw=−P(2Lx2​−6x3​)+C2​, and w(0)=0 gives C2​=0.
  3. So w(x)=−6EIPx2(3L−x)​ and the tip deflection is w(L)=−3EIPL3​.
  4. Numbers: P=1 kN, L=2 m, steel E=210 GPa, rectangular section 50×100 mm so I=bh3/12=4.167×10−6 m4. Tip deflection: 3×210×109×4.167×10−61000×8​=3.05 mm.

The code checks steps 1 to 3 symbolically: it substitutes the hand result back into the differential equation and both boundary conditions.

What a checker can and can’t do

  • It can confirm algebra, derivatives, integrals and that a function satisfies a differential equation and its boundary conditions.
  • It can’t tell you that you picked the wrong model. If the beam is short and thick, Euler–Bernoulli theory itself is off (shear deformation matters), and SymPy will happily confirm a correct derivation of the wrong equation.
  • Don’t use it to skip the derivation. The check only means something when you had a result to check.

Exercise 1Twice the length

The same cantilever is made 4 m long, everything else unchanged. Predict the new tip deflection using the formula’s structure, then confirm with numbers.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Tip deflection is PL3/(3EI), so it scales with L3.
  2. Doubling L multiplies it by 23=8.
  3. 8×3.05=24.4 mm.
  4. Direct: 3×210×109×4.167×10−61000×64​=24.4 mm. Same answer, and a reminder that long cantilevers get floppy fast.

sections.title: Equal means “the difference simplifies to zero”
A derivative you can’t look up quickly
What a checker can and can’t do

quiz.q: Evaluate the derivative of xx at x=2.
quiz.explain: xx(lnx+1)=4(ln2+1)=6.773.

quiz.q: Tip deflection of a 2 m steel cantilever (E=210 GPa, I=4.167×10−6 m4) under a 1 kN tip load, in mm.
quiz.explain: PL3/(3EI)=3.05 mm.

quiz.q: simplify(a - b) returns a non-zero expression. What can you conclude?
quiz.explain: Simplification isn’t guaranteed to find every identity; a numeric spot check settles it.
options: a and b are definitely different
Either they differ or SymPy didn’t find the simplification, so check numerically

quiz.q: Which step lets you differentiate xx?
quiz.explain: lny=xlnx turns the exponent into a product.

quiz.explain: Deflection scales with L3.

00.12.title: The Swiss rail timetable problem
00.12.html:
Swiss trains run on a clock-face timetable: the same departures every hour, with trains meeting at hub stations just before the full or half hour so passengers can change in a few minutes. That only works if every run between two stations takes a predictable time. This lesson models one run with nothing but constant-acceleration kinematics and closes Phase 00 by putting the whole loop together: derive, code, test.

Three phases of a run

A train leaves a station at rest, accelerates at a up to the line speed vmax​, cruises, then brakes at b to stop at the next platform a distance D away. For constant acceleration the distance covered while reaching speed v from rest is

s=2av2​.

So accelerating to vmax​ takes s1​=vmax2​/(2a) and braking from it takes s3​=vmax2​/(2b). If s1​+s3​≤D, the train cruises over the rest and the run time is

T=avmax​​+vmax​D−s1​−s3​​+bvmax​​=vmax​D​+2vmax​​(a1​+b1​).

The first term is the time at full speed over the whole distance. The second is the penalty for starting and stopping. If the stations are too close to reach line speed (s1​+s3​>D), the profile is a triangle with peak

vp​=a+b2Dab​​,T=vp​(a1​+b1​).

Worked exampleA regional run between two stations

Two stations are 8 km apart. A regional train has line speed 125 km/h, accelerates at 0.7 m/s2 and brakes at 0.9 m/s2.

  1. Line speed in SI: vmax​=125/3.6=34.72 m/s.
  2. Distances: s1​=34.722/1.4=861 m, s3​=34.722/1.8=670 m. Their sum, 1531 m, is less than 8000 m, so the train reaches line speed.
  3. Time: T=34.728000​+234.72​(0.71​+0.91​)=230.4+44.1=274.5 s, or 4 min 34 s.
  4. Add a 30 s dwell time at the station and a few percent recovery margin, and the timetable slot is about 5 min 20 s.

Raising line speed to 160 km/h gives T=236.4 s: 28% more speed buys only 14% less time on this short hop. Better acceleration is often the cheaper upgrade, which is why modern multiple units have powered axles along the whole train.

Simulate it and test against the formula

The formula is short, but the simulation is what you’d extend later with gradients, curves and traction limits. The test is that the two agree to 10−6 s. To get that accuracy the simulator doesn’t rely on a tiny time step: within each step it solves exactly for the moment a phase ends.

Exercise 1Stations close together

An S-Bahn stops every 1 km in the city, with the same train (vmax​=125 km/h, a=0.7, b=0.9 m/s2). Does it reach line speed? What peak speed and run time do you get?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Reaching 125 km/h needs s1​+s3​=1531 m>1000 m, so no: the profile is a triangle.
  2. Peak speed: vp​=0.7+0.92×1000×0.7×0.9​​=787.5​=28.06 m/s=101 km/h.
  3. Run time: T=28.06(0.71​+0.91​)=28.06×2.540=71.3 s.
  4. Line speed doesn’t matter at all on this stretch; only acceleration and braking do.
